btos.label: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21)

name: Mining
blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports mining-sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.name: USGS anchors the exploration data layer

points.name: Earth MRI maps the country for critical minerals

points.name: Rio Tinto runs the operations proof point

points.desc: One of the two dominant mining-equipment makers publishes its autonomous haulage and fleet-management technology - where operational AI ships as machinery.
points.name: Komatsu documents the autonomous equipment layer

points.name: NMA is the US trade association

points.desc: The International Council on Mining and Metals tracks ESG standards, automated safety monitoring, and digital transformation across the major international operators.
points.name: ICMM sets the global operator standards

points.name: Barrick and Newmont apply AI to gold

points.name: GeologicAI and Plotlogic scan the rock itself

summary: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling are the established deployments in a sector that adopted automation early. Mining AI splits into two horizons: exploration - long-term forecasting from satellite, magnetic, and core-scan data toward drilling targets - and site operations, where sensor streams and telemetry drive machinery, maintenance, and safety minute by minute.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 7.2% of firms in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction reported using AI in the most recent survey period, down from 7.9% in the prior period. That measured dip is worth noting alongside the broader context: mining is a sector that automated earlier than most, and the headline figure captures only two-week active use across all firm sizes, so it likely understates deployment at the largest operators where capital and technical capacity concentrate.

The clearest operational proof points come from major international producers. Rio Tinto operates autonomous haul trucks and drills at scale, representing what day-to-day AI looks like in production mining rather than in pilot programs. Komatsu, one of the two dominant mining-equipment makers, has entered a strategic partnership with AIM Intelligent Machines for autonomous operation of bulldozers and hydraulic excavators, embedding AI capability directly into the machinery layer that operators purchase. This means for many mines, AI arrives bundled with the equipment rather than as a separate software decision.

On the exploration side, KoBold Metals applies machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits including copper, cobalt, lithium, and nickel, and is developing Mingomba in Zambia, described as one of the world's largest copper mines. The public data infrastructure underpinning this kind of work comes substantially from the USGS Mineral Resources Program, which serves as the authoritative source of mineral resource information including production statistics and supply chain data, and from the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which is systematically re-mapping US geology with modern geophysics to support prospectivity work on critical minerals.

Specialist vendors are turning geology itself into machine-readable inputs. GeologicAI combines RGB, XRF, hyperspectral, and LiDAR sensors for core scanning and logging, and counts Agnico Eagle among its users, with the company stating that Agnico Eagle uses its scanning services to help make more confident decisions throughout the mining cycle. Freeport-McMoRan applies machine-learning models to processing, focused on maximizing mill throughput and ore recovery at existing copper operations. Newmont, per its technology record, uses AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring.

The International Council on Mining and Metals tracks digital transformation and safety standards across major international operators, and its 2025 safety report reflects a continued emphasis on technology as a tool for reducing fatalities and workplace hazards. The National Mining Association, as the official voice of US mining before Congress and federal agencies, navigates the regulatory environment that shapes how quickly domestic operators can deploy and scale these technologies. The Society for Mining, Metallurgy and Exploration publishes the working-group research on AI and machine learning in mineral processing that practitioners draw on.

For an operator weighing deployment, the sector evidence suggests that the highest-confidence use cases are autonomous haulage at large open-pit operations, computer-vision core scanning for geological consistency, and ML-driven mill optimization, all of which have named large-scale users rather than only vendor claims. Smaller firms face a meaningful gap: the capital requirements for autonomous equipment and the data volumes needed for useful ML models both favor operators with large, long-lived assets. The regulatory and ESG layer, shaped by bodies like ICMM and NMA, adds a compliance dimension that is itself increasingly data-intensive, which may create an additional incentive for AI adoption in reporting and monitoring even at operations not yet ready for autonomous equipment.
